questions.stem: Picture the situation: Store A sells 6 bus passes for $24 while Store B sells 5 for $40. Which store has the lower price per item?

options.text: Store B, at $40 per item.
options.misconception: compares total prices instead of price per unit

options.text: It cannot be determined from the totals given.
options.misconception: claims the unit prices cannot be calculated

options.text: Both stores charge exactly the same per item.
options.misconception: assumes equal unit costs without dividing

options.text: Store A, at $4 per item.

questions.explanation: Dividing each total by its quantity gives $4 per item at Store A and $8 at Store B, so the lower unit price determines the better value. Comparing only the totals or refusing to divide ignores the quantity difference.
questions.hint: Divide each total price by its quantity.

questions.stem: The decision: An item priced at $175 is marked down by 30%. What is the sale price?

options.misconception: reports the discount amount rather than the sale price
divides instead of multiplying by the remaining fraction
adds the discount instead of subtracting it

questions.explanation: A 30% markdown leaves 70% of the original price, so the sale price is $122.5. The discount amount, the inverted calculation, or a price increase each fails to give what the buyer actually pays.
questions.hint: Multiply by one minus the discount rate.
